articles.background: Autonomous and AI-assisted systems are developing faster than international rules. Existing humanitarian law applies to warfare, but states disagree over whether new, specific obligations are needed.
articles.whyItMatters: A binding instrument could establish clearer limits on human control, testing, accountability and the protection of civilians. Failure to agree could leave regulation fragmented.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the meeting's decision on a negotiating mandate, the positions of military powers and any proposal for meaningful human control.

articles.title: Oil prices ease as IEA forecasts fourth-quarter supply surplus despite Gulf shipping risks
articles.summary: Brent crude fell to about $95.30 a barrel on Monday as traders weighed the IEA's forecast that fourth-quarter supply will exceed demand by 1.7 million barrels per day.
articles.content: Oil prices slipped on Monday after the International Energy Agency forecast that global supply would average 105 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter of 2026, around 1.7 million barrels per day above demand. Reuters reported Brent at about $95.30 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate at about $88.34 in early trading. The IEA's outlook reflects the recovery of Gulf exports and weaker Chinese refinery demand, while the agency said 71 million barrels from emergency reserves would be available by the end of February. The market remains vulnerable: attacks and security concerns around the Strait of Hormuz have kept shipping costs high, and Iran's claim that a tanker hit a mine was not independently verified in the Reuters report. A forecast surplus does not guarantee lower retail fuel prices, because exchange rates, refining margins, taxes, transport costs and geopolitical risk also influence what households pay.

articles.background: Oil supply has been affected by the Gulf conflict and shipping disruption, while high prices have also restrained demand. The IEA's outlook has shifted from an expected deficit to a projected surplus.
articles.whyItMatters: For oil exporters such as Nigeria, price movements affect public revenue, foreign exchange and budget planning. For consumers, global crude prices are only one part of the final pump price.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch the IEA's next monthly outlook, OPEC+ production, Chinese refinery demand and security developments in the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Burnham's youth-employment plan puts training, job guarantees and welfare reform under scrutiny
articles.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has backed early intervention and a six-month skills-matched job guarantee for eligible 18-to-24-year-olds after a year on Universal Credit, while an independent review is expected to propose wider reforms.
articles.content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged a broader early-intervention approach to youth unemployment, including vocational training in schools and support before young people become detached from education or work. The Guardian reports that a taxpayer-funded scheme would guarantee eligible 18-to-24-year-olds a six-month, skills-matched job after a year on Universal Credit. The proposal is linked to an expected review by Alan Milburn, which is examining the number of young people not in education, employment or training and the role of employers, benefits and apprenticeships. Burnham says benefits should act as a backstop rather than a starting point, while critics will want to know whether temporary placements lead to lasting jobs and whether support is adequate for disabled young people. The final review has not yet been published, and the reported proposals should not be treated as enacted policy.

articles.background: Youth unemployment, inactivity and skills shortages have become major policy challenges in the UK. The government is reviewing how education, benefits and employers can help young people into work.
articles.whyItMatters: The test will be whether new placements deliver sustained employment, training and progression rather than short-term statistical improvements.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the Milburn review, funding details, eligibility rules and the government's response.

articles.title: Burnham says Brexit has not worked as UK prepares for a new EU agreement
articles.summary: Andy Burnham is expected to argue for closer UK-EU cooperation on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility ahead of the 20 November summit in Brussels. Any agreement remains under negotiation.
articles.content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to say that Brexit has not worked as promised and that the UK should pursue a more practical relationship with the European Union. The Guardian reports that he plans to seek agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility at a summit with EU leaders on 20 November. Burnham has argued that reducing trade barriers could support business and growth, while the government says any package must respect its manifesto commitments and deliver tangible benefits. European Commission and Council leaders will also weigh the costs of alignment, governance and the question of tuition fees for European students. This is a negotiating position, not a completed agreement or a decision to rejoin the EU. Former prime minister David Cameron and Brexit supporters continue to oppose making closer integration a priority.

articles.whatHappensNext: Watch the 20 November summit, any joint declaration and whether the proposed deals have agreed legal texts, costs and implementation dates.

articles.title: French public-sector unions prepare 17 November strike after talks with Lecornu stall
articles.summary: The CFDT has joined the 17 November public-sector strike call after the government postponed purchasing-power negotiations until 11 December. The dispute adds pressure on Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.
articles.content: French public-sector unions are preparing a strike and demonstrations on 17 November after talks with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu failed to produce a timetable for immediate negotiations on pay and purchasing power. TV5MONDE, citing AFP, reports that the CFDT joined the mobilisation after the government postponed discussions until 11 December. The government has announced measures intended to bring the lowest public-sector salaries closer to the minimum wage, but unions say these do not address wider pay erosion or the cost of living. The dispute follows weeks of demonstrations involving students, workers and other groups. Le Monde reported that the government mobilised 70,000 police and gendarmes for earlier demonstrations on 14 November. The strike's actual scale and its impact on transport, schools and public services will become clearer on the day; service disruptions should not be assumed in advance.

articles.title: Estonia plans to close road crossings with Russia from 1 December after alleged sabotage attempt
articles.summary: Estonia says it will close its remaining road border crossings with Russia from 1 December after an alleged arson and sabotage attempt. The announcement raises border-security concerns but is not a declaration of war.
articles.content: Estonia has announced that it will close its remaining road border crossings with Russia from 1 December after authorities reported an attempted arson attack and a suspected sabotage plot. Reuters reported that the decision follows heightened concern about security along the eastern border. The announcement is a border-control measure; it does not amount to a declaration of war or prove that the Russian state directed the alleged operation. The specific evidence, suspects and any charges should be assessed through the Estonian authorities' investigation and subsequent court proceedings. The move comes amid wider European concerns about sabotage, cyber operations and the security of critical infrastructure following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Travellers and freight operators will need to plan for the loss of road-crossing options and use official border-service information.

articles.title: Carney says Canada could seek Chinese, European or Japanese automakers if US trade talks fail
articles.summary: Mark Carney says negotiations with Washington remain his priority, but Canada may seek alternative investment if US trade talks fail. Any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial Canadian manufacturing and supply chains.
articles.content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in Manila that talks with the United States remain Canada's priority, but their outcome could determine whether Ottawa pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. Carney said any Chinese investment would need substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simple assembly of imported vehicles, with labour standards, local facilities and domestic supply chains. The comments come as President Donald Trump presses automakers to shift production to the United States and cross-border vehicle supply chains face tariff uncertainty. Canada has already lowered its tariff on a limited number of Chinese electric vehicles under a January arrangement, while China agreed to reduce tariffs on Canadian agricultural products including canola. Ontario Premier Doug Ford has criticised the deal, warning of risks to Canadian jobs and access to the US market. Carney's remarks describe a possible contingency, not a signed new investment agreement.

articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the next round of US-Canada trade talks, any formal investment proposals and reactions from Ontario's auto industry.

articles.title: DR Congo's Ebola outbreak exceeds 11,000 confirmed cases as response remains under pressure
articles.summary: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reported 11,197 confirmed cases and 5,471 deaths in the DRC as of 12 November, based on data through 11 November. Community transmission continues.
articles.content: The Bundibugyo-virus Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains a major public-health emergency. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control's 13 November update reported 11,197 confirmed cases and 5,471 related deaths in the DRC, using data through 11 November. Eight provinces had been affected, with community transmission ongoing. The ECDC said an additional 83 confirmed cases and 38 deaths were reported in the period covered by its latest update. Separately, Africa CDC's director-general warned that the outbreak remained serious and difficult to control, with many new cases outside monitored contact lists and a large share of deaths occurring in communities. Response work is complicated by insecurity, limited resources, delays in care and attacks on health workers. The ECDC also reported one case in Nigeria, whose patient was medically evacuated to Switzerland, and nine confirmed cases in Kenya. These figures are time-stamped and may change as national data are reconciled.

articles.title: Ethiopia and Sudan close consulates amid disputed claims of support for armed groups
articles.summary: The neighbours have exchanged consulate closures and expulsions amid accusations of interference in each other's conflicts. Both governments deny the allegations; the diplomatic expulsions are confirmed.
articles.content: Ethiopia and Sudan have closed each other's consulates near their shared border, escalating diplomatic tensions in the Horn of Africa. Reuters reported that Ethiopia ordered Sudanese consular staff in Assosa to leave, after which Sudan closed Ethiopia's consulate in Gedaref and expelled its staff. Sudan accuses Ethiopia of allowing the Rapid Support Forces to use Ethiopian territory for drone attacks on civilian infrastructure. Addis Ababa denies supporting the RSF. Ethiopia has also accused Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea of backing Tigrayan rebels; the countries named have denied those allegations. Sudan says it raised its complaint with the UN Security Council and the African Union's Peace and Security Council. The allegations have not been independently established in the reporting reviewed. The confirmed development is the reciprocal consulate closures and worsening diplomatic relations. Sudan's war between the national army and the RSF, which began in April 2023, continues to produce mass displacement and severe humanitarian needs.

articles.title: EU weighs a proposed €45 billion Ukraine loan backed by its budget
articles.summary: The European Commission is preparing a proposal for a €45 billion loan using the EU budget as backing. It remains a proposal and would require agreement by member states and the relevant EU institutions.
articles.content: The European Commission is preparing a proposal for a €45 billion loan to Ukraine backed by the EU budget, according to the Financial Times. The proposal is part of efforts to maintain financial support for Kyiv as the war continues and as questions remain over the future of other financing mechanisms. The amount is not an approved disbursement: member states and EU institutions would still need to agree on the legal and budgetary terms. The debate involves the distribution of financial risk among member states, the timing of payments and how the loan would fit with existing EU and G7 commitments. Ukraine's government needs predictable financing for public services and defence, while European governments face domestic budget constraints and political disagreements about the scale and form of support.

articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the Commission's formal proposal, member-state negotiations and the legal conditions attached to any loan.

articles.title: Kenya discharges its last Ebola patient and begins 42-day countdown to possible outbreak-free declaration
articles.summary: Kenya says its last Ebola patient has been discharged. If no new infections are detected, the required 42-day monitoring period could end on 23 December.
articles.content: Kenya has discharged its final Ebola patient, starting the 42-day surveillance period required before the country can declare the outbreak over. The Associated Press reports that Kenya recorded nine confirmed cases and two deaths after an infected traveller arrived from the Democratic Republic of the Congo via Uganda. Seven patients recovered, and the country's authorities say identified contacts completed monitoring. If no new infections occur, the countdown could end on 23 December. The development is encouraging for Kenya but does not mean the wider regional outbreak has ended: the DRC continues to report a much larger Bundibugyo-virus outbreak, and health agencies are maintaining border and community surveillance. Kenya has urged other governments to assess the epidemiological evidence carefully when considering travel measures affecting its citizens.

articles.title: Nafiu Bala Gombe offers conditional reconciliation to Atiku and David Mark as ADC crisis deepens
articles.summary: Nafiu Bala Gombe, whose lawsuit produced the 5 November judgment against the David Mark-led ADC leadership, says he is open to reconciliation but insists that party membership and constitutional procedures must be followed. The rival factions have not announced an agreement.
articles.content: Former ADC deputy national chairman Nafiu Bala Gombe has offered to work with former vice-president Atiku Abubakar, former Senate president David Mark and other prominent figures amid the party's leadership dispute. His proposed reconciliation is conditional: he says those seeking leadership or nomination must meet the party constitution's membership, ward-registration and dues requirements. Gombe's lawsuit led to the Federal High Court judgment of 5 November setting aside the processes that produced the Mark-led leadership and decisions taken under it, including Atiku's nomination. The Mark-led faction has appealed and sought a stay of execution. Those steps do not automatically suspend the judgment, and no appellate order granting a stay or final appeal outcome was verified at midday. INEC has said it will examine the judgment and take legal advice. Neither faction has announced a settlement or an agreed route for resolving the leadership and nomination questions.

articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for a formal reconciliation proposal, further court filings, INEC's position after reviewing certified documents and any decision on the stay application.

articles.title: NDC challenges Tinubu administration over health and defence budget releases; APC rejects criticism
articles.summary: The Nigeria Democratic Congress has questioned capital releases to health and defence and contrasted them with political publicity and donations. The APC dismissed the criticism. The NDC has not supplied evidence that political donations were funded with public money.
articles.content: The NDC says capital funding for essential services deserves greater scrutiny. Its spokesperson cited a figure disclosed by Health Minister Muhammad Pate to lawmakers in February: only ₦36 million released from a ₦218 billion 2025 capital allocation to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare. The NDC also alleged that about seven per cent of the defence capital budget was released, but that figure was not independently confirmed against official budget records in the reporting reviewed. The party questioned the apparent availability of resources for political publicity and gifts distributed by groups supporting President Bola Tinubu. It has not produced records establishing that those donations were financed with government funds. APC national publicity secretary Felix Morka dismissed the NDC's criticism as political grandstanding and accused it of monitoring the governing party rather than preparing for the election. His response did not provide alternative capital-release figures. The health allocation figure is attributed to the minister's parliamentary disclosure; the defence figure and any alleged link between public funds and political donations remain unverified.

articles.title: Kwankwaso's team alleges convoy attack in Kano; state government disputes account
articles.summary: Rabiu Kwankwaso's team says suspected thugs targeted its campaign convoy in Kano. The state government disputes reports of an attack; the allegation has not been independently established.
articles.content: Reports published on 16 November say members of Rabiu Kwankwaso's political team alleged that suspected thugs targeted a campaign convoy in Kano. The Kano State Government disputed the account. The available reporting does not establish the identities of any attackers, the precise circumstances or whether a police investigation has confirmed an assault. The allegation comes days after a separate disruption of Peter Obi's NDC town-hall meeting in Lagos, an incident also marked by competing political claims and denials. The two incidents should not be treated as connected without evidence. Political parties should preserve video and witness evidence and report threats to law enforcement. Security agencies should publish verified findings and protect campaign activity across party lines.

articles.title: Trump's Asia visit begins under pressure after US midterm defeat and China technology allegations
articles.summary: Donald Trump is heading to Manila and Shenzhen after his party's midterm losses. Meetings with regional leaders and Xi Jinping will test a fragile trade truce amid disputes over advanced chips and allegations involving Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
articles.content: Reuters reports that President Donald Trump's Asia trip is unfolding after a Republican midterm defeat and allegations that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had links to a suspected Chinese spy. Trump is due to meet Southeast Asian leaders in Manila before travelling to Shenzhen for the APEC forum and talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping. A three-way discussion involving Vladimir Putin has also been reported as planned, but its agenda and outcome should not be assumed in advance. Washington is seeking to preserve a fragile trade truce while US lawmakers consider tighter restrictions on China's access to advanced semiconductors. Beijing rejects the spy allegations as a pretext for a technology blockade. The allegations about Huang are not, by themselves, proof of wrongdoing; the reporting describes scrutiny and political controversy, not a judicial finding. The trip also takes place amid pressure over North Korea diplomacy, Taiwan arms sales and the wider regional balance.

articles.background: The United States and China remain deeply interdependent in trade while competing over technology, security and influence in the Indo-Pacific.
articles.whyItMatters: Any breakdown in the trade truce or escalation in semiconductor restrictions could affect global supply chains, investment and regional security.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the Manila meetings, the APEC agenda, official statements after any Trump-Xi meeting and any confirmed agreements on trade, chips or regional security.

articles.title: Russia seeks senior posts at UN telecoms agency as Moscow pursues influence in digital governance
articles.summary: Russia is seeking senior positions at the UN telecommunications agency in Geneva. Diplomats say the effort could help Moscow reduce diplomatic isolation and shape debates over digital technology.
articles.content: Reuters reports that Russia is seeking senior posts at the International Telecommunication Union, the UN agency responsible for telecommunications and aspects of global digital governance. The contest matters because technical standards, spectrum allocation, connectivity policy and the governance of emerging technologies have significant geopolitical and commercial consequences. Diplomats quoted by Reuters describe the effort as part of Moscow's attempt to rebuild influence at multilateral institutions despite its isolation over the war in Ukraine. The election of agency officials is a formal multilateral process; the candidacies themselves do not establish that Russia will win the positions or gain control of the organisation. The result will be one indicator of how member states balance technical cooperation with political concerns about Russia's conduct.

articles.background: International technical agencies increasingly sit at the intersection of communications infrastructure, cybersecurity, digital rights and geopolitical competition.
articles.whyItMatters: Leadership choices can influence standards and governance priorities that affect countries far beyond the states competing for senior posts.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the ITU election results and the positions taken by member states on candidates and digital governance priorities.

articles.title: Alibaba launches Qwen4-Max flagship AI model with expanded professional and scientific capabilities
articles.summary: Alibaba says its new Qwen4-Max model is designed for complex professional and scientific work, with upgraded safety protections. Independent performance comparisons were not included in the initial announcement.
articles.content: Reuters reports that Alibaba unveiled Qwen4-Max on 15 November, describing it as its new flagship artificial-intelligence model. The company says the system is intended to handle a broad range of creative and professional tasks, including 3D modelling, game development, precision manufacturing, finance, law and healthcare, and that it has improved safety protections. These are the developer's claims and should not be treated as independently verified performance results. Meaningful assessment will require technical documentation, independent benchmarks, evaluations of reliability and security, and information about access, pricing and deployment. The launch adds to competition among Chinese and US technology firms as governments debate chip access, AI safety and export controls.
articles.imageNote: Technology illustration only; not a photograph of the Qwen4-Max model.
articles.background: AI competition is increasingly shaped by model capability, access to advanced chips, safety testing and national industrial policy.
articles.whyItMatters: Claims about model capability affect investment and policy decisions. Independent testing is needed to distinguish product marketing from demonstrated performance.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for independent benchmark results, technical papers, availability announcements and responses from competitors and regulators.

articles.title: France's 2027 presidential election dates trigger constitutional and political debate
articles.summary: France's proposed presidential election dates of 18 April and 2 May 2027 are drawing criticism because the second round would fall immediately after the 1 May public holiday and union demonstrations. The dates still require formal confirmation by decree.
articles.content: Le Monde reports that the planned first and second rounds of France's 2027 presidential election — 18 April and 2 May — have triggered a debate about constitutional timing and public order. Conservative Bruno Retailleau has called 2 May a potential date of chaos, while centre-left figure Raphaël Glucksmann has also supported reconsideration. The government opposes changing the timetable, arguing that postponement in response to possible disorder would create a dangerous precedent. The Constitution requires the election to take place within a defined period before Emmanuel Macron's term ends on 14 May, leaving a narrow choice of dates. The proposed schedule has not yet been formally confirmed by decree. Criticism of the timetable is political argument, not evidence that the election will be postponed.
articles.imageNote: Repository portrait; story concerns election timetable, not a photograph of a current event.
articles.background: France's next presidential election is taking shape amid fragmentation across the centre, left and right and disputes over the rules governing the transition.
articles.whyItMatters: Election dates affect campaign planning, voter access and public confidence. The constitutional timetable limits the government's options and makes formal confirmation important.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the decree formally setting the dates and for further reactions from political parties, unions and constitutional experts.

articles.title: Le Pen's National Rally proposes major cuts to public-interest organisations and union funding
articles.summary: Le Monde reports that Marine Le Pen's National Rally is proposing restrictions on public funding for nonprofits it considers political, alongside cuts affecting unions. Critics warn the proposals could weaken civil-society scrutiny.
articles.content: Le Monde's 13 November analysis describes a National Rally programme that would seek to reduce public funding for associations the party considers political or politicised, with a proposed reduction of around €4 billion, and to cut support for unions. The party argues that organisations wishing to express political views should enter electoral politics rather than receive public funding. Critics say the approach could weaken charities, research organisations and civil-society groups that monitor government or defend minority rights. The report also describes confrontations between RN figures and judges, journalists and constitutional institutions. These are proposals and political statements, not enacted policy. The debate is relevant to France's 2027 election because it concerns the independence of institutions that scrutinise whoever holds power.
articles.imageNote: Repository portrait; proposal coverage, not an event photograph.
articles.background: The National Rally is seeking to broaden its appeal ahead of the 2027 presidential election while facing scrutiny over its approach to checks and balances.
articles.whyItMatters: Public funding rules can affect the independence of charities, unions and watchdog organisations. Proposals should be examined for their legal basis, impact and safeguards against selective enforcement.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the party's detailed programme, responses from affected organisations and constitutional scrutiny of any legislation if adopted.

articles.title: Nigeria's annual inflation eases to 14.06% in October, but food prices remain high
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Statistics reported headline inflation of 14.06% year-on-year in October, down from 14.63% in September. Food inflation eased to 19.13%, but household costs remain elevated.
articles.content: Nigeria's annual headline inflation rate eased to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September, according to the National Bureau of Statistics data reported by Reuters on Monday. Food inflation also slowed, from 19.59% to 19.13%. The figures offer some relief after months in which inflation remained close to 15%, but they do not mean prices have returned to earlier levels or that households have recovered lost purchasing power. A slower rate of increase means prices are rising less quickly; it does not mean food, transport, energy and other essentials have become cheaper. The Tinubu administration has argued that its reforms, including ending the petrol subsidy and changing the exchange-rate regime, are intended to strengthen public finances and the economy. Those measures have also contributed to higher costs for consumers. The political test ahead of the 2027 election will be whether lower inflation is sustained and translates into improved living standards, jobs and real incomes.
articles.imageAlt: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu; portrait used to illustrate the government's economic policy context
articles.imageNote: Official-leader repository portrait; not a photograph of the NBS data release.
articles.background: Nigeria has faced a prolonged cost-of-living crisis following major changes to fuel pricing and foreign-exchange policy. Inflation data is one of the main measures used to assess whether price pressures are easing.
articles.whyItMatters: Food inflation remains above headline inflation and directly affects household budgets. The distinction between slower inflation and falling prices is essential when assessing claims of economic recovery.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch the next NBS inflation release, food-price movements, exchange-rate conditions, transport and energy costs, and whether real wages begin to recover.

articles.title: Nigeria's state-police amendment advances after 32 state assemblies approve the bill
articles.summary: Senate Leader Opeyemi Bamidele says 32 state assemblies have approved the constitutional alteration bill. Four states are expected to submit their positions by 17 November; details of the final framework remain unclear.
articles.content: The proposed constitutional amendment to establish state police has moved closer to the next legislative stage after Senate Leader Opeyemi Bamidele said at least 32 state Houses of Assembly had approved the bill. The National Assembly says this meets the two-thirds threshold required under Section 9(2) of the Constitution. Bamidele said four remaining assemblies were expected to submit their reports by 17 November, when lawmakers reconvene. The PUNCH reported that parliamentary sources believed the number could have risen to 34, but the public record described by the Senate Leader still referred to 32 approvals and four outstanding reports. The final text and practical design remain important questions: who will appoint and supervise state police commissioners, how will funding be shared, what safeguards will prevent political misuse, and how will state forces coordinate with federal police? The amendment process is not the same as an operational state-police service. Any constitutional change must complete the required formal steps, including presidential assent and implementation legislation.

articles.imageNote: Leader portrait; not an image of the bill or a parliamentary sitting.

articles.background: Calls for decentralised policing have intensified amid persistent kidnappings, banditry and communal violence. The Constitution currently places the Nigeria Police Force under federal control.
articles.whyItMatters: State policing could bring law enforcement closer to local communities, but without strong oversight it could also expose officers to pressure from governors and local political interests.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch the outstanding state resolutions, the final bill text, the National Assembly's transmission process and the safeguards proposed for appointments, funding, investigations and human rights.

articles.title: Cape Verde President José Maria Neves wins second term in provisional results
articles.summary: Provisional results from 97% of polling stations put Neves on 63.8%, ahead of Joana Rosa on 31.6%. Rosa conceded; official results are expected later this week. Turnout appeared low.
articles.content: Cape Verde's incumbent president José Maria Neves has won a second five-year term, according to provisional results from 97% of polling stations reported by Reuters. Neves received 63.8% of the vote, while his main challenger, former justice minister Joana Rosa, received 31.6%. Rosa conceded defeat and said her campaign as the country's first female presidential candidate could help advance equality. Neves has pledged to raise wages, tackle poverty and strengthen opportunities for Cape Verdeans living at home and abroad. Turnout appeared to be below one-third, prompting debate about voter engagement, youth emigration and the electoral register. Neves has suggested updating voter registration and considering electronic voting. The provisional count is not the final certified result; official results are expected later in the week. Cape Verde is often regarded as one of West Africa's more stable democracies, but the departure of young people seeking work abroad remains a major national challenge.
articles.imageAlt: Regional illustration representing Cape Verde and West Africa
articles.imageNote: Regional illustration only; not a photograph of the candidates or polling stations.
articles.background: Cape Verde is an Atlantic island state with a population of about half a million and a large diaspora, particularly in the United States and Portugal.
articles.whyItMatters: The result reinforces the incumbent's mandate, while low participation and emigration underline long-term pressures on democratic engagement and economic opportunity.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch the final certified result, turnout data, the president's policy priorities and whether proposals to modernise voter registration proceed.

articles.title: Marine Le Pen defends plan to end French financial aid to Ukraine if elected
articles.summary: Le Pen says a National Rally government would end French financial support for Ukraine within six months of a victory in May 2027. Macron has warned that cutting aid could pressure Ukraine into an unjust peace.
articles.content: Marine Le Pen has defended a proposal to end French financial aid to Ukraine within six months if the National Rally wins the 2027 presidential election. Le Monde reports that she declined an invitation from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to visit Kyiv and was instead due to meet Ukraine's ambassador to France. Le Pen argues that France's public finances cannot sustain the current level of support. Her party says it may continue some material assistance or training, while ending direct bilateral contributions and France's share of European aid schemes. Le Monde cites estimates that France has contributed about €27 billion to Ukraine's war effort since 2022 through bilateral and European channels. President Emmanuel Macron criticised those who, in his view, would ration Ukraine's resources and risk forcing it into an unjust peace. Le Pen's proposal is an election position, not current government policy. Its implementation would depend on an electoral victory, the powers of the presidency and government, parliamentary decisions and France's European commitments.
articles.imageAlt: Marine Le Pen, leader of the National Rally
articles.imageNote: Repository portrait; story concerns her stated election policy, not a photograph of the ambassador meeting.
articles.background: France is a major European supporter of Ukraine. The 2027 presidential campaign is increasingly focused on public finances, sovereignty, security and the future of European cooperation.
articles.whyItMatters: A change in French policy could affect Ukraine's military and financial position and test the unity of the European Union at a critical stage of the war.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch the meeting with Ukraine's ambassador, further details from the RN campaign, Macron's response and the positions of other French presidential candidates.

articles.title: Sweden urges EU to develop a new plan to use frozen Russian assets for Ukraine
articles.summary: Sweden wants the European Commission to share the financial risks of moving frozen Russian assets out of Belgium and using them to support Ukraine. The proposal remains under discussion.
articles.content: Sweden has called on the European Commission to prepare a new proposal for using frozen Russian assets to help finance Ukraine, with Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard arguing that financial risks should be shared among EU member states. She told Euronews that Belgium should not carry the burden alone if the assets are moved or used through a new financing mechanism. The debate is legally and politically sensitive because the assets are frozen under sanctions and any use of principal raises questions about sovereign immunity, financial stability and possible retaliation. Sweden says bilateral support for Ukraine has declined and that Europe must maintain military and financial assistance while seeking a seat at any future peace negotiations. The proposal is not an adopted EU decision. Member states remain divided over the legal route and the distribution of risk. The European Commission is also preparing a separate budget-backed loan proposal for Ukraine, which should not be confused with a final agreement to use frozen Russian assets.
articles.imageAlt: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen
articles.imageNote: Repository portrait illustrating the EU policy debate; not a photograph of the Swedish minister.
articles.background: The EU has frozen large amounts of Russian state assets following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Belgium hosts a major financial clearing house holding a substantial share of those assets.
articles.whyItMatters: The outcome could shape Ukraine's ability to finance defence and reconstruction while setting precedents for sanctions, sovereign assets and the distribution of financial risk within the EU.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for a Commission proposal, legal assessments, Belgium's position and whether member states can agree on a common risk-sharing arrangement.

articles.title: China and ASEAN leaders pledge restraint but fail to conclude South China Sea code
articles.summary: Leaders meeting in Manila pledged to avoid actions that could escalate maritime disputes, but negotiations on a South China Sea code remain unfinished after more than two decades.
articles.content: China and Southeast Asian leaders have pledged to avoid actions that could escalate disputes in the South China Sea, but they have not completed a long-negotiated code of conduct for the contested waters. The Associated Press reports that roughly 80% of the draft text has been agreed, while key questions remain over the code's geographic scope, the meaning of sensitive terms and whether it will be legally binding. The talks involve China and ASEAN states, including the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, whose claims overlap in parts of the sea. The waterway is a major route for international trade and energy shipments. Recent confrontations between Chinese and Philippine vessels have kept tensions high. The pledge to exercise restraint is a diplomatic signal, not a settlement of sovereignty claims or a binding guarantee against future incidents. Negotiations are expected to continue under Singapore's ASEAN chairmanship next year.
articles.imageNote: General regional illustration; not a photograph of the Manila summit.

sources.name: Al Jazeera — ASEAN and China fall short of agreeing on South China Sea code

articles.background: The South China Sea is claimed in whole or in part by several governments and is one of the world's busiest maritime trade corridors.
articles.whyItMatters: Without agreed rules and effective crisis communication, maritime encounters can disrupt trade or escalate into a wider confrontation involving regional powers and the United States.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for the next negotiating timetable, the legal status proposed for the code and any new maritime incidents or joint statements.

articles.title: Carney says Canada may seek Chinese or other automakers if US trade talks fail
articles.summary: Mark Carney says Canada still prioritises negotiations with Washington but could pursue partnerships with Chinese, European or Japanese automakers if US trade measures undermine the integrated North American industry.
articles.content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canada may look to Chinese, European or Japanese automakers if negotiations with US President Donald Trump fail to protect an integrated North American automotive industry. Speaking in Cambodia ahead of a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Carney said talks with Washington remain his priority but that US trade measures have weakened cross-border production links. He said any Chinese investment must involve substantial manufacturing in Canada, strong labour standards, local facilities and deeper supply chains using Canadian critical minerals, rather than simply assembling imported parts. Canada and China reached a January agreement that reduced Canada's tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1% for an initial annual quota of 49,000 vehicles, while China lowered tariffs on some Canadian agricultural products. Ontario Premier Doug Ford has warned that the arrangement could threaten local jobs and complicate access to the US market. The policy debate reflects Canada's attempt to diversify trade while protecting its most important export relationship.
articles.imageNote: Repository portrait of the Canadian prime minister; not a photograph of the Cambodia meeting.
articles.background: Canada's automotive sector is closely integrated with US manufacturing. Tariffs and industrial policy changes have raised uncertainty for vehicle makers and workers on both sides of the border.
articles.whyItMatters: A shift in investment could reshape North American supply chains, Canadian employment and the balance between economic diversification and access to the US market.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch Carney's meeting with Xi, the next round of US-Canada trade talks, the details of any investment conditions and reactions from Ontario's automotive sector.

articles.title: UN Geneva talks expose deep divisions over legally binding limits on autonomous weapons
articles.summary: 128 states are considering whether to negotiate rules for lethal autonomous weapons. The US, Russia and Israel oppose a binding pact, while the UK, Germany and France support talks on a possible instrument.
articles.content: Governments meeting in Geneva under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons are debating whether to begin negotiations on rules for lethal autonomous weapons systems. Reuters reports that 128 states parties are considering the issue. The United States, Russia and Israel oppose a legally binding pact, arguing that existing international humanitarian law is sufficient; Washington favours non-binding guidelines and has proposed a five-year mandate. The meeting chair has proposed a two-year negotiation mandate for a binding protocol, while the UK, Germany and France support negotiations on an instrument whose final legal form remains open. Russia initially objected to a rule allowing observers, including the European Union and non-governmental organisations, to speak. UN Secretary-General António Guterres has urged states to establish clear prohibitions and restrictions, citing humanitarian, legal, ethical and security risks. The debate concerns weapons that can select and attack targets without meaningful human control; it is not a general ban on artificial intelligence in defence. No treaty has been agreed.
articles.imageAlt: Illustrative image representing artificial intelligence and autonomous systems
articles.imageNote: Technology illustration; not a photograph of a weapon system or Geneva negotiations.
articles.background: Diplomats have debated autonomous weapons for years as advances in sensors, robotics and AI make systems capable of identifying and engaging targets with less direct human involvement.
articles.whyItMatters: The rules could determine how international humanitarian law applies to emerging weapons and who is accountable when an autonomous system causes civilian harm.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch the Geneva meeting's final decision on a mandate, the positions of major military powers and whether states can agree on meaningful human control and enforceable safeguards.

articles.title: Gulf markets recover as Bahrain reports Iranian attacks and tanker fire raises Hormuz fears
articles.summary: Gulf stock markets recovered from early losses despite heightened security concerns. Iran says a tanker caught fire after striking a mine in the Strait of Hormuz; the mine account has not been independently verified.
articles.content: Most Gulf stock markets recovered from early losses on Monday despite renewed security concerns after Bahrain reported intercepting Iranian aerial attacks and Iran said a tanker had caught fire after striking a mine in the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters said the mine report could not be independently verified. Saudi Arabia's index rose 0.1%, while Dubai and Abu Dhabi each gained 0.2%; Qatar's benchmark climbed 2.6% after a previous-session decline. Investors remained cautious about possible disruption to Gulf shipping and the wider conflict involving Iran, the United States and Israel. The Associated Press separately reported Iranian claims that naval mines had set several oil tankers ablaze, alongside other regional incidents; those claims should be distinguished from independently confirmed facts. The Strait of Hormuz is a critical route for global oil and gas shipments, so even limited disruption can raise insurance costs, freight rates and energy-price volatility. Market movements do not mean the security risk has passed.
articles.imageAlt: Regional illustration for Middle East security and Gulf shipping
articles.imageNote: Regional illustration only; not a photograph of the reported tanker fire or attack.
articles.background: The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and is a vital passage for global energy exports.
articles.whyItMatters: A prolonged disruption could increase global oil prices, shipping insurance and transport costs, affecting import-dependent economies and consumers.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch independent maritime incident reporting, official statements from Gulf states, shipping advisories, oil prices and any diplomatic effort to reduce hostilities.

articles.title: UK prime minister prepares to call for a reset in relations with the European Union
articles.summary: Andy Burnham is expected to argue that the Brexit settlement has not delivered as promised and set out three tests for a closer EU relationship ahead of the 20 November summit.
articles.content: The United Kingdom's prime minister, Andy Burnham, is expected to use the Lord Mayor's Banquet in London to call for a reset in relations with the European Union. Sky News and the Guardian report that he plans to argue that the Brexit settlement created unnecessary barriers for businesses and weakened the UK's economic potential. His stated tests for any future agreement are that it must remain consistent with the government's manifesto and red lines, improve on the original Brexit deal, and deliver tangible benefits in everyday life. Areas under discussion ahead of Friday's UK-EU summit include food standards, emissions trading and youth mobility. Ministers have indicated that primary legislation may be required, potentially delaying implementation until 2028. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has criticised the renewed debate, while the Liberal Democrats have accused the government of avoiding a clear position. The speech is a political statement and negotiating direction; it does not mean the UK is rejoining the EU or that any new treaty has been concluded.
articles.imageNote: Repository portrait of the UK prime minister; not a photograph of the Lord Mayor's Banquet.
articles.background: The UK left the EU in 2020. Since then, governments have debated how to reduce trade friction and cooperate on security, energy and migration without reversing the referendum result.
articles.whyItMatters: A closer relationship could affect trade costs, labour mobility, energy markets and the political balance between sovereignty and economic cooperation.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch the full speech, the 20 November summit, the proposed negotiating timetable and reactions from business groups and opposition parties.

europeNews.title: Sudan detains former ruling-party chief Ahmed Haroun, wanted by the ICC over Darfur allegations
europeNews.summary: Two party officials and lawyers say Haroun has been detained; the reason and his current whereabouts were not immediately clear.
europeNews.content: Sudan's military authorities have detained Ahmed Haroun, a former senior official under ousted president Omar al-Bashir, according to party officials and lawyers. Haroun is wanted by the International Criminal Court over allegations of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur in the early 2000s. Those are charges, not a conviction by the ICC. Reports say the reason for the latest detention was unclear, and neither the military nor the court had immediately commented. Haroun previously escaped prison after it was attacked during the current war. The detention is significant because it raises questions about accountability for past atrocities while Sudan remains engulfed in a separate conflict between the army and the Rapid Support Forces. Any transfer to the ICC or formal domestic proceedings would require clear legal steps and confirmation from the relevant authorities.
europeNews.imageNote: Regional illustration only; not a photograph of Ahmed Haroun
europeNews.background: Haroun was a senior figure in Bashir's government, which was accused of atrocities in Darfur. The ICC has outstanding warrants connected to that period.
europeNews.whyItMatters: Accountability for past crimes is difficult to separate from the current struggle for power and the protection of civilians in Sudan.
europeNews.whatHappensNext: Watch for confirmation of the detention, legal grounds, access to counsel and any communication from the ICC.

europeNews.title: France's presidential contest sharpens as Le Pen leads polls and public-sector unions prepare strike
europeNews.summary: A recent poll places Marine Le Pen ahead of potential rivals, while the CFDT has joined a public-sector strike call for 17 November. Polls are snapshots, not election results.
europeNews.content: France's 2027 presidential contest is taking shape amid social unrest and a fragmented field of potential candidates. A Financial Times report published on 15 November says Marine Le Pen is polling at about 36% in a first-round scenario, ahead of Jean-Luc Mélenchon and centrist rivals including Édouard Philippe. The result reflects one poll and should not be treated as a prediction of the eventual election. The same political climate is being shaped by public-sector wage disputes: the CFDT joined a strike call for 17 November after talks with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu failed to satisfy unions. President Emmanuel Macron cannot seek another consecutive term, and potential candidates across the centre, left and right are debating whether to unite or compete separately. Le Pen's legal history and any appeal proceedings remain separate from polling and must be reported on their own terms.

europeNews.whyItMatters: A fragmented centre and left could alter the likely runoff contest, while industrial action tests the government's capacity to negotiate.
europeNews.whatHappensNext: Watch for the 17 November strike, new polling, party decisions on primaries and any court developments affecting candidate eligibility.

europeNews.title: Germany's 2027 budget plan clears committee with near-record borrowing
europeNews.summary: Parliamentary budget committee approved a €561 billion spending plan and €210.4 billion in new borrowing; a parliamentary vote is still required.
europeNews.content: Germany's parliamentary budget committee has approved a 2027 spending plan worth €561 billion, clearing it for a vote in parliament. The package includes €210.4 billion in new borrowing, the second-highest amount since the Second World War, just below the pandemic-era record. The coalition government says the spending is needed to support infrastructure, defence and social cohesion. Negotiations exposed differences between Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats and their Social Democrat partners: proposals for a plastics tax and welfare cuts were dropped or delayed, and a planned electricity-tax reduction was postponed over funding disagreements. The Alternative for Germany criticised the borrowing as a debt spree, while some CDU members also questioned concessions made to the coalition partner. The committee decision is not the final parliamentary vote, and the fiscal consequences will depend on economic growth, spending delivery and future budgets.

europeNews.background: Germany is expanding defence and infrastructure spending while debating how to finance the investment and maintain fiscal credibility.
europeNews.whyItMatters: The budget will influence Europe's largest economy and the EU's capacity to fund security, industrial competitiveness and infrastructure.
europeNews.whatHappensNext: Watch the Bundestag vote, coalition negotiations and the government's explanation of how borrowing will be allocated.

europeNews.title: UK and EU prepare 20 November summit on security, migration and trade barriers
europeNews.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is due to meet EU leaders in Brussels and says he wants practical agreements to reduce costs and red tape for businesses and farmers.
europeNews.content: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is scheduled to meet European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on 20 November for the second UK-EU summit. Downing Street says the discussions will review progress since the strategic partnership agreed at the first summit and identify practical steps on security, illegal migration, crime and economic cooperation. Burnham has said he wants agreements that cut paperwork and costs for farmers, food producers and businesses. The summit will not itself reverse Brexit or guarantee a new trade agreement; any changes will depend on negotiated commitments and their implementation. The meeting is an important test of whether the UK and EU can improve day-to-day cooperation while maintaining their separate legal and political arrangements.

europeNews.background: The UK left the EU, but the two sides remain close trading and security partners. Both have faced pressure to reduce trade friction and manage irregular migration.
europeNews.whyItMatters: Practical cooperation could affect food prices, business costs, border security and the wider European response to geopolitical risks.
europeNews.whatHappensNext: Watch the summit statement, any commitments on food standards and mobility, and the timetable for implementing agreed measures.

europeNews.title: Burnham's youth-employment plan puts training, job guarantees and welfare reform under scrutiny
europeNews.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has backed early intervention and a six-month skills-matched job guarantee for eligible 18-to-24-year-olds after a year on Universal Credit, while an independent review is expected to propose wider reforms.
europeNews.content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged a broader early-intervention approach to youth unemployment, including vocational training in schools and support before young people become detached from education or work. The Guardian reports that a taxpayer-funded scheme would guarantee eligible 18-to-24-year-olds a six-month, skills-matched job after a year on Universal Credit. The proposal is linked to an expected review by Alan Milburn, which is examining the number of young people not in education, employment or training and the role of employers, benefits and apprenticeships. Burnham says benefits should act as a backstop rather than a starting point, while critics will want to know whether temporary placements lead to lasting jobs and whether support is adequate for disabled young people. The final review has not yet been published, and the reported proposals should not be treated as enacted policy.

europeNews.background: Youth unemployment, inactivity and skills shortages have become major policy challenges in the UK. The government is reviewing how education, benefits and employers can help young people into work.
europeNews.whyItMatters: The test will be whether new placements deliver sustained employment, training and progression rather than short-term statistical improvements.
europeNews.whatHappensNext: Watch for the Milburn review, funding details, eligibility rules and the government's response.

africaNews.title: Cape Verde President José Maria Neves wins second term in provisional results
africaNews.summary: Provisional results from 97% of polling stations put Neves on 63.8%, ahead of Joana Rosa on 31.6%. Rosa conceded; official results are expected later this week. Turnout appeared low.
africaNews.content: Cape Verde's incumbent president José Maria Neves has won a second five-year term, according to provisional results from 97% of polling stations reported by Reuters. Neves received 63.8% of the vote, while his main challenger, former justice minister Joana Rosa, received 31.6%. Rosa conceded defeat and said her campaign as the country's first female presidential candidate could help advance equality. Neves has pledged to raise wages, tackle poverty and strengthen opportunities for Cape Verdeans living at home and abroad. Turnout appeared to be below one-third, prompting debate about voter engagement, youth emigration and the electoral register. Neves has suggested updating voter registration and considering electronic voting. The provisional count is not the final certified result; official results are expected later in the week. Cape Verde is often regarded as one of West Africa's more stable democracies, but the departure of young people seeking work abroad remains a major national challenge.

africaNews.title: Guinea reports at least ten deaths during clashes linked to illegal-mining crackdown
africaNews.summary: Authorities say the crackdown targets illegal extraction and environmental damage; the circumstances of the deaths and responsibility for individual shootings remain contested.
africaNews.content: At least ten people were killed during clashes in Guinea after security forces moved against artisanal mining activity, according to reporting by the Associated Press. Authorities have defended the operation as an effort to curb illegal extraction and environmental harm. The crackdown has involved arrests and restrictions around mining areas, while local residents and miners have raised concerns about livelihoods and the conduct of security personnel. The precise circumstances of each death, including who fired particular shots, require independent investigation. Guinea is a major producer of bauxite and has significant mineral resources, but informal mining is also a source of income for communities with limited alternatives. A sustainable response needs enforcement against environmental damage alongside transparent procedures, due process and credible options for affected workers.

africaNews.title: DR Congo Ebola outbreak passes 11,000 reported cases as health services struggle
africaNews.summary: Government figures reported 11,042 cases and at least 5,387 deaths by 10 November in an outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo strain.
africaNews.content: Government data reported 11,042 Ebola cases and at least 5,387 deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo by 10 November. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain and has affected eight of the country's 26 provinces. Health authorities face delayed detection, insecurity and strained medical services, with many deaths occurring outside treatment centres. The Bundibugyo strain does not have a licensed vaccine or specific treatment comparable to those available for some other Ebola strains. The World Health Organization has approved clinical trials of two vaccine candidates, with results expected in 2027. These figures are serious and should be dated because outbreak totals can change as cases are investigated and records reconciled. The response requires infection prevention, safe burial practices, contact tracing, community trust and access for health workers.

africaNews.whatHappensNext: Watch WHO situation reports, vaccine-trial updates, case definitions and official cross-border preparedness measures.

africaNews.title: Senegal confirms 39 deaths after migrant boat disaster off Lompoul
africaNews.summary: Senegal's official reporting puts the death toll at 39, with one survivor; the investigation and search for missing people remain important.
africaNews.content: Senegal's official news agency reported that the death toll from a migrant boat disaster off Lompoul had risen to 39, with one survivor. The vessel was attempting a dangerous Atlantic crossing toward the Canary Islands, a route used by people seeking to reach Europe. Early reports gave lower casualty figures as rescue and recovery operations continued; the updated official figure should be used with its source and date. The tragedy is part of a wider pattern in which people risk overcrowded and poorly equipped boats because of limited economic opportunities, insecurity and the hope of finding work abroad. The immediate priorities are identifying victims, supporting families, establishing what happened to the vessel and investigating any trafficking or smuggling networks. Longer-term responses require safe migration pathways and credible economic opportunities at home.

africaNews.title: Ethiopia and Sudan close each other's consulates amid reciprocal accusations over armed groups
africaNews.summary: The confirmed development is the reciprocal closure of consulates; claims that either government supports armed groups are disputed and not independently established.
africaNews.content: Ethiopia and Sudan have closed each other's consulates near their shared border, escalating tensions between two countries already affected by conflict. Ethiopia ordered six Sudanese consular staff in Assosa to leave within 48 hours; Sudan then closed Ethiopia's consulate in Gedaref and expelled its staff. Sudan accuses Ethiopia of allowing the Rapid Support Forces to use Ethiopian territory to launch drones against infrastructure. Ethiopia denies supporting the RSF and has accused Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea of backing Tigrayan rebels; those governments reject the accusations. Sudan says it has lodged complaints with the UN Security Council and the African Union's Peace and Security Council. These allegations remain contested. The confirmed facts are the diplomatic expulsions and the worsening relationship. The risk is that the conflicts in Sudan and northern Ethiopia become more closely connected, worsening humanitarian conditions and regional instability.

africaNews.whyItMatters: A diplomatic rupture could affect border trade, humanitarian access and the risk of cross-border escalation.

africaNews.title: DR Congo's Ebola outbreak exceeds 11,000 confirmed cases as response remains under pressure
africaNews.summary: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reported 11,197 confirmed cases and 5,471 deaths in the DRC as of 12 November, based on data through 11 November. Community transmission continues.
africaNews.content: The Bundibugyo-virus Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo remains a major public-health emergency. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control's 13 November update reported 11,197 confirmed cases and 5,471 related deaths in the DRC, using data through 11 November. Eight provinces had been affected, with community transmission ongoing. The ECDC said an additional 83 confirmed cases and 38 deaths were reported in the period covered by its latest update. Separately, Africa CDC's director-general warned that the outbreak remained serious and difficult to control, with many new cases outside monitored contact lists and a large share of deaths occurring in communities. Response work is complicated by insecurity, limited resources, delays in care and attacks on health workers. The ECDC also reported one case in Nigeria, whose patient was medically evacuated to Switzerland, and nine confirmed cases in Kenya. These figures are time-stamped and may change as national data are reconciled.

africaNews.title: Kenya discharges its last Ebola patient and begins 42-day countdown to possible outbreak-free declaration
africaNews.summary: Kenya says its last Ebola patient has been discharged. If no new infections are detected, the required 42-day monitoring period could end on 23 December.
africaNews.content: Kenya has discharged its final Ebola patient, starting the 42-day surveillance period required before the country can declare the outbreak over. The Associated Press reports that Kenya recorded nine confirmed cases and two deaths after an infected traveller arrived from the Democratic Republic of the Congo via Uganda. Seven patients recovered, and the country's authorities say identified contacts completed monitoring. If no new infections occur, the countdown could end on 23 December. The development is encouraging for Kenya but does not mean the wider regional outbreak has ended: the DRC continues to report a much larger Bundibugyo-virus outbreak, and health agencies are maintaining border and community surveillance. Kenya has urged other governments to assess the epidemiological evidence carefully when considering travel measures affecting its citizens.

nigeriaNews.title: Nigeria's annual inflation eases to 14.06% in October, but food prices remain high
nigeriaNews.summary: The National Bureau of Statistics reported headline inflation of 14.06% year-on-year in October, down from 14.63% in September. Food inflation eased to 19.13%, but household costs remain elevated.
nigeriaNews.content: Nigeria's annual headline inflation rate eased to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September, according to the National Bureau of Statistics data reported by Reuters on Monday. Food inflation also slowed, from 19.59% to 19.13%. The figures offer some relief after months in which inflation remained close to 15%, but they do not mean prices have returned to earlier levels or that households have recovered lost purchasing power. A slower rate of increase means prices are rising less quickly; it does not mean food, transport, energy and other essentials have become cheaper. The Tinubu administration has argued that its reforms, including ending the petrol subsidy and changing the exchange-rate regime, are intended to strengthen public finances and the economy. Those measures have also contributed to higher costs for consumers. The political test ahead of the 2027 election will be whether lower inflation is sustained and translates into improved living standards, jobs and real incomes.

nigeriaNews.background: Nigeria has faced a prolonged cost-of-living crisis following major changes to fuel pricing and foreign-exchange policy. Inflation data is one of the main measures used to assess whether price pressures are easing.
nigeriaNews.whyItMatters: Food inflation remains above headline inflation and directly affects household budgets. The distinction between slower inflation and falling prices is essential when assessing claims of economic recovery.
nigeriaNews.whatHappensNext: Watch the next NBS inflation release, food-price movements, exchange-rate conditions, transport and energy costs, and whether real wages begin to recover.

nigeriaNews.title: Nigeria's state-police amendment advances after 32 state assemblies approve the bill
nigeriaNews.summary: Senate Leader Opeyemi Bamidele says 32 state assemblies have approved the constitutional alteration bill. Four states are expected to submit their positions by 17 November; details of the final framework remain unclear.
nigeriaNews.content: The proposed constitutional amendment to establish state police has moved closer to the next legislative stage after Senate Leader Opeyemi Bamidele said at least 32 state Houses of Assembly had approved the bill. The National Assembly says this meets the two-thirds threshold required under Section 9(2) of the Constitution. Bamidele said four remaining assemblies were expected to submit their reports by 17 November, when lawmakers reconvene. The PUNCH reported that parliamentary sources believed the number could have risen to 34, but the public record described by the Senate Leader still referred to 32 approvals and four outstanding reports. The final text and practical design remain important questions: who will appoint and supervise state police commissioners, how will funding be shared, what safeguards will prevent political misuse, and how will state forces coordinate with federal police? The amendment process is not the same as an operational state-police service. Any constitutional change must complete the required formal steps, including presidential assent and implementation legislation.

asiaNews.title: China and ASEAN leaders pledge restraint but fail to conclude South China Sea code
asiaNews.summary: Leaders meeting in Manila pledged to avoid actions that could escalate maritime disputes, but negotiations on a South China Sea code remain unfinished after more than two decades.
asiaNews.content: China and Southeast Asian leaders have pledged to avoid actions that could escalate disputes in the South China Sea, but they have not completed a long-negotiated code of conduct for the contested waters. The Associated Press reports that roughly 80% of the draft text has been agreed, while key questions remain over the code's geographic scope, the meaning of sensitive terms and whether it will be legally binding. The talks involve China and ASEAN states, including the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, whose claims overlap in parts of the sea. The waterway is a major route for international trade and energy shipments. Recent confrontations between Chinese and Philippine vessels have kept tensions high. The pledge to exercise restraint is a diplomatic signal, not a settlement of sovereignty claims or a binding guarantee against future incidents. Negotiations are expected to continue under Singapore's ASEAN chairmanship next year.

asiaNews.whatHappensNext: Watch for the next negotiating timetable, the legal status proposed for the code and any new maritime incidents or joint statements.

asiaNews.title: ASEAN summit opens in Manila with Myanmar, energy security and South China Sea tensions on the agenda
asiaNews.summary: Leaders begin three days of meetings as the Philippines seeks practical regional cooperation on security, energy, food, migration and economic resilience.
asiaNews.content: The 49th ASEAN Summit and related meetings begin in Manila on 15 November and run through 17 November under the Philippines' 2026 chairmanship. The official programme places food and energy security, regional stability, migrant workers' welfare and transnational crime among the central themes. The gathering comes as fuel-importing economies across Southeast Asia face higher energy costs linked to the wider Middle East conflict. Myanmar remains a difficult test for the bloc: leaders are expected to review progress on ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus, while the country continues to experience a devastating internal conflict after the 2021 military coup. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has said ASEAN will continue what he calls constructive and principled engagement with Myanmar. The summit is also a venue for talks with major partners, including China, the United States, Australia, Canada and India. The discussions matter because ASEAN's ability to speak collectively is being tested by security disputes, divergent national interests and pressure to protect trade routes.

asiaNews.title: Philippines and Australia sign defence cooperation arrangement amid South China Sea tensions
asiaNews.summary: The agreement is designed to reduce administrative delays in joint military activity and expand maritime awareness, training and disaster-response cooperation.
asiaNews.content: The Philippines and Australia signed a defence cooperation arrangement in Manila on 15 November. Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said the arrangement would simplify implementation of the two countries' Status of Visiting Forces Agreement and make joint activities easier to organise. The cooperation covers maritime, air and land forces, humanitarian assistance and disaster response. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the agreement would strengthen information sharing, training, interoperability and maritime-domain awareness; Australia also announced additional investment in drones, equipment and training. Manila presents the agreement as part of its effort to strengthen deterrence in the South China Sea. Beijing rejects the 2016 international arbitral ruling that found no legal basis for China's expansive claims and has criticised joint military activities involving the Philippines and its partners. The new arrangement does not itself resolve the maritime disputes, but it deepens the security network around the waterway.

asiaNews.title: China-ASEAN South China Sea code remains unfinished after Manila summit
asiaNews.summary: The Manila summit ended without completing the long-negotiated code of conduct with Beijing. The failure leaves maritime dispute management unresolved.
asiaNews.content: ASEAN leaders concluded their Manila summit on Sunday without completing the long-negotiated South China Sea code of conduct with China. The Philippines had hoped to finalise the text during its chairmanship, but maritime disputes and differences among member states remain unresolved. Chinese Premier Li Qiang praised economic ties with the bloc, citing more than US$1 trillion in annual trade in the previous year and more than US$500 billion in cumulative investment. Economic interdependence has not removed security disagreements. The code is intended to reduce the risk of incidents and provide a framework for managing disputes, but it has not yet been concluded. The summit's outcome is therefore a continuation of negotiations, not a new binding agreement.

asiaNews.background: The South China Sea is a major shipping route and a source of overlapping territorial claims involving China and several Southeast Asian states.
asiaNews.whyItMatters: Without agreed rules and effective crisis communication, encounters between coast guards, fishing vessels and military ships can escalate.
asiaNews.whatHappensNext: Watch for renewed negotiations and any maritime incident reports during the next round of regional diplomacy.

asiaNews.summary: The Manila summit closed on Sunday without completing a long-negotiated South China Sea code of conduct. China praised ties with ASEAN as Donald Trump prepared to arrive in Manila before the APEC meeting in Shenzhen.
asiaNews.content: The 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations concluded its leaders' summit in Manila on Sunday without finalising the long-negotiated code of conduct with China intended to manage disputes in the South China Sea. The Philippines, which chairs ASEAN this year, had hoped to complete the agreement, but maritime disputes and differing national positions remain unresolved. Chinese Premier Li Qiang described relations with ASEAN as strong and cited more than US$1 trillion in annual trade last year and more than US$500 billion in cumulative two-way investment. The bloc also maintained its policy of excluding Myanmar's military rulers from summit-level meetings unless there is sustained and concrete progress on the ASEAN peace plan. US President Donald Trump is due in Manila on Tuesday, where he is expected to meet ASEAN leaders and take part in a Quad gathering with Japan, Australia and India, before travelling to Shenzhen for the APEC forum. A possible meeting involving Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has been reported as planned for the APEC sidelines, but its agenda and any outcome remain unconfirmed.

businessNews.title: Carney says Canada may seek Chinese or other automakers if US trade talks fail
businessNews.summary: Mark Carney says Canada still prioritises negotiations with Washington but could pursue partnerships with Chinese, European or Japanese automakers if US trade measures undermine the integrated North American industry.
businessNews.content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canada may look to Chinese, European or Japanese automakers if negotiations with US President Donald Trump fail to protect an integrated North American automotive industry. Speaking in Cambodia ahead of a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Carney said talks with Washington remain his priority but that US trade measures have weakened cross-border production links. He said any Chinese investment must involve substantial manufacturing in Canada, strong labour standards, local facilities and deeper supply chains using Canadian critical minerals, rather than simply assembling imported parts. Canada and China reached a January agreement that reduced Canada's tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1% for an initial annual quota of 49,000 vehicles, while China lowered tariffs on some Canadian agricultural products. Ontario Premier Doug Ford has warned that the arrangement could threaten local jobs and complicate access to the US market. The policy debate reflects Canada's attempt to diversify trade while protecting its most important export relationship.

businessNews.whatHappensNext: Watch Carney's meeting with Xi, the next round of US-Canada trade talks, the details of any investment conditions and reactions from Ontario's automotive sector.
